abstract.para: CPU scheduling is the kernel mechanism that controls how execution time on processor cores is allocated among competing processes and threads. Because a system typically has far more running tasks than physical or logical CPU cores, the kernel scheduler acts as an arbiter, deciding which thread gets to run, when it runs, for how long, and on which specific CPU core.

topic.para: The primary objective of the kernel is to provide predictability, determinism, and bounded dispatch latency. To achieve this, real-time CPU scheduling controls two complementary dimensions of thread execution: timing and placement (on which CPU core a task runs).

Controlling the timing dimension is handled by real-time scheduling policies and real-time priority levels. These settings ensure that whenever a time-critical task is ready to execute, the real-time scheduler immediately preempts lower-priority workloads.

However, real-time priority alone does not restrict a task to a specific processor. By default, the scheduler may migrate a running thread between available CPU cores to balance the overall system load. In real-time environments, this migration introduces unwanted latency through context switching, cache invalidation, and non-uniform memory access (NUMA) penalties.

To eliminate migration overhead and guarantee deterministic execution, scheduling policies must be paired with CPU affinity. While scheduling policies determine preemption rights on a given core, CPU affinity pins tasks to dedicated cores, preserving cache locality and isolating critical execution paths from the rest of the operating system.
